newsitem.title: USA: 100,000 still powerless after New England storms.
newsitem.headline: 100,000 still powerless after New England storms.

text.p: Some 100,000 households were still without power on Tuesday, more than three days after two storms roared through New England burying the region in snow and rain and killing five people.

Some 650 emergency crews from Canada, New York, New Jersey and Pennsylvania were working around the clock trying to restore power to various New England utilities' customers. About 100 people huddled in emergency shelters in southern New Hampshire communities because of power outages, state Office of Emergency Management spokeswoman Dena Deluca said.
More people in Massachusetts found refuge -- and heat -- in four shelters in the central part of the state, Renita Hosler of the Massachusetts Red Cross said.

The storms on Friday and Saturday blanketed the region with up to 24 inches (61 cm) of heavy, wet snow that felled trees and powerlines. With temperatures dropping into the low 20s (-5 C), the melting snow froze, making it more difficult for crews to reach fallen powerlines, one Nashua, New Hampshire, town offical said.
Northeast Utilities reported 26,400 Connecticut customers were still without power, as were 22,000 in New Hampshire and 2,800 in western Massachusetts.

"We're hoping to get 99 percent of those in Connecticut back by midnight (Tuesday) and most of those in western Massachusetts and New Hampshire back by 6 p.m. EST (2300 GMT) on Wednesday," Northeast spokeswoman Susan Millerick said. "But there are some areas of New Hampshire where there was total devastation and there it looks like Thursday or beyond."

Public Service of New Hampshire, the state's largest electric utility, estimated that 87,000 households were without power and it would take until Thursday before all customers were back on. A spokesman said damage to power lines from fallen limbs was more severe than initially suspected.
Boston Edison reported that 1,000 of its customers remained without power as well. Meanwhile, the death toll from the weekend storms was fixed at five.

New Hampshire state police said David Blodgett, 34, was killed when his snowmobile crashed on Saturday and Richard Stone, 78, died on his roof of an apparent heart attack while shoveling snow. Donald Farley, 53, of Manchester died when he was struck by a snow-laden tree branch. Michelle Amaru, 40, of Hinsdale died in a car crash on snow-slicked Route 119.

Connecticut state police said a volunteer firefighter in Somers was killed early on Sunday when he stepped on a power line while putting out a fire at a neighbour's house. Craig Arnone, 23, died after the oxygen tank he was wearing came in contact with a downed electrical line carrying 23,000 volts.

The weekend storms were also blamed for two house fires in New Hampshire. Fire officials said residents in the houses in Hudson and Hooskett, N.H. used faulty fireplaces and stoves to try to keep warm, when the homes exploded in flames.

Meanwhile, the Coast Guard, which had rescued three crewmembers of a fishing vessel off the coast of Massachusetts during the height of Friday's storm, reported on Tuesday that the ship and its captain, one crewmember and a golden retriever had all made it safely to back to port.
